analysis.one_liner: Bars federal agencies from regulating greenhouse gas emissions unless Congress expressly authorizes it.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in May 2010 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The LEASE Act would have prohibited the head of any federal agency — including the EPA — from taking any action to regulate, monitor, mitigate, predict, or even document greenhouse gas emissions for climate purposes unless a federal statute expressly and specifically authorized it. Its stated target was the Bureau of Land Management's decision to suspend 61 Montana-area oil and gas leases while it studied their climate effects. The bill never moved past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies holding federal leases — the bill's findings name the suspended 2008 lease sales in Montana, North Dakota, and South Dakota — plus any industry whose emissions would otherwise face EPA limits. Blocking agency action would have kept those lease sales on schedule and kept climate rules off the books until Congress chose to write them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal oil and gas lessees; heavy-emitting industries

how_it_helps.text: It would have barred every federal agency from regulating, monitoring, mitigating, predicting, or documenting greenhouse gas emissions for climate purposes without an express, specific statutory mandate, stopping rules even short of formal regulation.

It was written in response to the Bureau of Land Management's agreement, in a lawsuit settlement, to suspend 61 oil and gas leases issued in 2008 while it conducted further environmental analysis, and its postponement of 2010 lease sales in Montana, North Dakota, and South Dakota.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who rely on federal air-quality and climate protections. If agencies could not act, curbing carbon pollution would depend entirely on Congress passing a statute — which would have left existing emissions rules and lease-review requirements without a backstop.
analysis.who_pays_short: Anyone breathing the air; future generations

drawbacks.text: The bill's ban on monitoring, predicting, and documenting emissions would have gone beyond blocking regulation — agencies could not even measure or report greenhouse gases for climate purposes without new legislation, a broader restriction than most agency-power objections target.

The good-faith case for it: major climate policy decisions with large economic effects were being made by agencies and through litigation settlements rather than by the elected Congress, and requiring express statutory authorization would put those choices back before voters' representatives. The acknowledged cost is that Congress has rarely passed such a statute, so the practical effect would likely be no greenhouse-gas limits at all.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The democratic-legitimacy argument — that Congress, not agencies or lawsuits, should set climate policy — has real force, but the bill's remedy was so broad that it would have eliminated even emissions monitoring and documentation, leaving no path to climate action short of new legislation. The costs to public health and climate protection would have outweighed the procedural gain.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee after its referral in May 2010 and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011, never reaching the floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Denny Rehberg, joined by Rep. Stephanie Herseth Sandlin, introduced the bill on May 13, 2010, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
Nine members cosponsored it: seven Republicans and two Democrats.
The referral was the bill's only action; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died in committee, federal agencies kept their existing authority to consider greenhouse gas emissions in lease reviews and emissions rules, and oil, gas, and coal interests failed to obtain the blanket exemption this bill would have given them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Everyone who relies on federal climate rules

for.name: Rep. Denny Rehberg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill responding to the suspension of 61 Montana-area oil and gas leases and referred it to Energy and Commerce.

for.name: Rep. Stephanie Herseth Sandlin
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor; the lease sales at issue covered her state as well as Montana and North Dakota.

for.name: 2 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Democratic support it drew.

against.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill's referral was its final action for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was 7 of 178 Republicans against 2 of 253 Democrats — nearly all Republican, with token Democratic backing.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies holding federal leases
industries.note: The bill's own findings identify the suspended 2008 lease sales in Montana, North Dakota, and South Dakota as its target; blocking agency climate analysis would have kept those leases and future sales moving. The public would have borne the unexamined climate and air-quality effects.

A bar on any agency action on greenhouse gases without explicit statutory authority would have shielded all major emitters from new EPA limits. The cost of that shield falls on everyone exposed to the emissions.

industries.industry: Environmental review and climate-science functions of federal agencies
industries.note: Agencies would have been barred from monitoring, predicting, or documenting emissions for climate purposes, sidelining the government's own analysis of climate effects.
